blocks.label: gray code recursive reflection (LC89)
blocks.py:
def gray(n):
    if n == 0: return [0]
    prev = gray(n - 1)
    return prev + [x | (1 << (n-1)) for x in reversed(prev)]
# closed form: g(i) = i ^ (i >> 1)

items.title: 4Sum II (MITM essence)
items.statement: Count tuples a+b+c+d=0 across four arrays: two half-sum hashmaps multiply-count.
hints: O(n²) beats O(n⁴) — say the exponent math.

solutionCode.label: meet in the middle: hash one half, probe with the other

items.complexity: Time O(n^2), space O(n^2). The brute force over four arrays is O(n^4) — at n = 200 that is 1.6 billion versus 40 thousand.

followups.a: Brute force tries every quadruple: n^4. Splitting into halves gives n^2 pairs on each side, and the join is a hash probe per pair — so n^2 to build plus n^2 to probe, total O(n^2). At n = 200 that is 1.6x10^9 versus 8x10^4, roughly a 20,000x reduction. The cost is O(n^2) memory, which is the trade meet-in-the-middle always makes.

followups.q: Why store counts rather than a set of sums?
followups.a: Multiple (a,b) pairs can produce the same sum, and each is a distinct tuple in the answer. A set would count each sum once and massively undercount. The value in the map is how many ways that sum can be formed — the multiplication is the whole point.

items.title: Subset Sum Count via MITM (CSES-style)
items.statement: n≤40 weights, count subsets hitting X exactly. Section trace generalized.
hints: Sort one half's sums for two-pointer join alternative.

solutionCode.label: split in half, enumerate both, join on the complement

items.complexity: Time O(2^(n/2) * n/2) for generation plus a sort or hash join. Space O(2^(n/2)). At n = 40 that is about a million per half instead of a trillion total.

followups.q: Why does splitting help so much at n = 40?
followups.a: 2^40 is about 10^12 — hours. Two halves of 20 give 2^20 ~ 10^6 each, generated in milliseconds, and the join is a hash lookup per left sum. Total ~2x10^6 operations. Meet-in-the-middle turns 2^n into 2^(n/2), which is the square root of the work.

followups.q: What is the two-pointer alternative to the hash join?
followups.a: Sort both halves, then walk one ascending and the other descending, counting matching runs. It is O(2^(n/2) log) for the sort but uses no hash table and has far better cache behaviour — often faster in practice despite the log. It also generalises to counting sums BELOW a bound, which hashing cannot do.

items.title: Gray Code Sequence
items.statement: Return any valid gray sequence; then verify adjacency programmatically.

solutionCode.label: reflect-and-prefix, plus the closed form

items.complexity: Time O(2^n) to emit 2^n codes. Space O(2^n) for the output.

followups.q: Why does reflection preserve the single-bit property?
followups.a: Within each copy of G(n-1) adjacency already holds. At the seam, the last element of the forward copy and the first of the reversed copy are the SAME value except the new high bit — so they differ in exactly one bit. Reversing is what makes the seam align; concatenating without reversing breaks it.

Incrementing i flips a suffix of bits 1...1 to 0...0 and carries. XOR-ing with the shifted value cancels all but the single boundary bit of that flip, so consecutive outputs differ in exactly one position. It is the same sequence as reflection, derived arithmetically rather than constructively.

items.title: Tower of Hanoi Move List
items.statement: Print optimal moves for n≤15 + state total = 2ⁿ−1.
hints: Count moves during run as assertion.

solutionCode.label: move n-1 aside, move the big disk, move n-1 back
solutionCode.py:
def hanoi(n: int, src: str = "A", dst: str = "C", aux: str = "B") -> list:
    moves = []

    def rec(k, frm, to, via):
        if k == 0:
            return
        rec(k - 1, frm, via, to)          # park the tower on the spare peg
        moves.append(f"{frm}->{to}")      # move disk k
        rec(k - 1, via, to, frm)          # bring it back onto the target

    rec(n, src, dst, aux)
    # the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 solves to exactly 2^n - 1
    assert len(moves) == (1 << n) - 1
    return moves

items.complexity: Time O(2^n) — exactly 2^n - 1 moves, which is provably optimal. Space O(n) recursion depth.

followups.a: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 with T(0) = 0. Expanding: T(n) = 2^n * T(0) + (2^(n-1) + ... + 2 + 1) = 2^n - 1. It is also provably minimal: the largest disk must move at least once, and before it can, all n-1 smaller disks must be on the spare peg — so any solution contains two full (n-1) solutions plus one move.

followups.q: Why is the aux peg argument rotated on each call?
followups.a: Because the roles change. In the first call the target becomes the spare; in the second the source becomes the spare. Getting the rotation wrong produces a plausible-looking move list that violates the "never place a larger disk on a smaller one" rule — which is why the test validates the moves against a real peg simulation, not just the count.

items.title: Target Sum (bridge to DP)
items.statement: ± assignments hitting S. Solve brute backtracking now; derive subset-transform formula; memoized version arrives Module 16.

solutionCode.label: brute backtracking, plus the transform that turns it into subset-sum
solutionCode.py:
def find_target_sum_ways_brute(a: list, S: int, i: int = 0, run: int = 0) -> int:
    """Sign every element; count assignments reaching S. O(2^n)."""
    if i == len(a):
        return 1 if run == S else 0
    return (find_target_sum_ways_brute(a, S, i + 1, run + a[i]) +
            find_target_sum_ways_brute(a, S, i + 1, run - a[i]))


def find_target_sum_ways(a: list, S: int) -> int:
    """TRANSFORM: P + N = total and P - N = S, so P = (total + S) / 2.
    The answer is the number of subsets summing to that value."""
    total = sum(a)
    if abs(S) > total:
        return 0                       # unreachable
    if (total + S) % 2:
        return 0                       # ODD PARITY: impossible
    need = (total + S) // 2

    dp = [0] * (need + 1)
    dp[0] = 1
    for x in a:
        for t in range(need, x - 1, -1):   # descending: 0/1 knapsack
            dp[t] += dp[t - x]
    return dp[need]

items.complexity: Brute force O(2^n). The algebraic transform reduces it to a subset-count DP in O(n * sum).

followups.a: Split the elements into P (given +) and N (given -). By construction P + N = total and P - N = S. Adding the equations gives 2P = total + S, so P = (total + S) / 2. Counting sign assignments becomes counting subsets with that exact sum — a standard 0/1 knapsack count.

followups.q: Why does odd parity mean zero immediately?
followups.a: P must be an integer sum of integers, so (total + S) must be even. If it is odd, no split exists and the answer is 0 without any search. That single parity check eliminates roughly half of all queries in O(1) — the cheapest possible prune.

items.title: Deep Recursion Survival Drill
items.statement: Rebuild linked-list length recursively at n=10⁶ without overflow-crash: options = iterative conversion / explicit stack / increased stack — measure each.
hints: Explicit-stack version mirrors unwind order exactly.

solutionCode.label: three survival strategies, measured rather than asserted

items.complexity: Naive recursion: O(n) stack, which dies around 10^4 frames in Python and 10^5-10^6 in C++. Explicit stack: O(n) heap, no limit. Iterative: O(1).

followups.q: Why does the explicit stack survive where recursion does not?
followups.a: Call frames live on the thread stack, which is a fixed reservation — 1 MB on Windows, 8 MB typical on Linux — and overflowing it is an immediate crash with no exception to catch. A vector or list lives on the heap, which grows to available RAM. Same O(n) space, radically different ceiling.

followups.q: When is the explicit stack the RIGHT answer rather than the iterative loop?
followups.a: When you actually need the unwind order — post-order tree traversal, or any algorithm where work happens after the recursive call returns. For a length count there is nothing to do on the unwind, so the loop is strictly better. Reaching for an explicit stack on a tail-recursive walk is converting one problem into a harder version of itself.
